lesson.title: Order of Operations: The Rules That Keep Math From Falling Apart
lesson.summary: PEMDAS is not an arbitrary rule to memorize, it is the agreed-upon sequence for reading a mathematical expression so that every person, and every calculator, arrives at the same single answer.
lesson.body:
Consider the expression 3 + 4 x 2. Read left to right with no rules at all, you might add first and get 7 x 2 = 14, or multiply first and get 3 + 8 = 11. Both paths seem reasonable, yet they give different answers, and a universal language for math cannot tolerate that kind of ambiguity. Order of operations exists to remove the ambiguity entirely: everyone, everywhere, agrees to multiply before adding, so 3 + 4 x 2 is always 11, no exceptions and no debate.

The standard order, often remembered by the acronym PEMDAS, is: parentheses (or any grouping symbols) first, then exponents, then multiplication and division together, working left to right, then addition and subtraction together, working left to right. The two 'together' pairs are the part students misremember most often. Multiplication does not always come before division just because M comes before D in the acronym, and addition does not always come before subtraction. Instead, whichever of that pair appears first when reading left to right gets done first. Treating PEMDAS as six separate, strictly ordered steps rather than four is a common source of avoidable ACT mistakes.

Work through 3 + 4 x (2 cubed minus 5) divided by 2 carefully. Parentheses first: inside them, evaluate the exponent, 2 cubed is 8, then subtract, 8 minus 5 is 3. The expression is now 3 + 4 x 3 divided by 2. Multiplication and division come next, left to right: 4 x 3 is 12, then 12 divided by 2 is 6. That leaves 3 + 6, and addition finishes the job: 9. Every step followed the hierarchy exactly, grouping symbols, then the exponent inside them, then multiplication and division in the order they appeared, then addition last.

This structure is what makes every later topic in this course reliable. When you plug a number into an equation, evaluate a function, or simplify inside a formula for slope or a derivative, you are relying on order of operations to guarantee that your calculation and the answer key's calculation land on the exact same number. A single misordered step early in a long problem can silently produce a wrong final answer even when every individual arithmetic fact used along the way was correct, which is exactly why this unglamorous topic deserves real attention before moving on to solving equations.
